title: Microsoft 365 tenant overview
summary: Understand what a Microsoft 365 tenant actually is, how its admin centers and licensing fit together, and where you go to support users as a Tier 2 cloud admin.
objectives: Explain what a Microsoft 365 tenant is and how it maps to a single organisation
Navigate the Microsoft 365 admin center and the specialist admin centers
Describe how licensing and subscriptions assign capabilities to users
Identify where domains, DNS, and Microsoft Entra ID fit into a tenant
Use admin roles to control who can change tenant settings
Locate the tenant ID and key settings needed to support and audit a tenant

options: A dedicated, isolated instance of Microsoft 365 services for one organisation
A physical server in a Microsoft data centre
A backup copy of a mailbox
quiz.why: A tenant is the dedicated, logically isolated instance of Microsoft 365 (Entra ID, Exchange, Teams, SharePoint, etc.) that belongs to one organisation and is identified by a unique tenant ID and default *.onmicrosoft.com domain.

quiz.q: Which admin center is the central starting point for managing users, licences, and other admin centers?
quiz.why: The Microsoft 365 admin center (admin.microsoft.com) is the hub: it manages users, groups, licences, and service health, and links out to the specialist admin centers.

quiz.q: What controls which Microsoft 365 capabilities a specific user can access?
options: The licences (subscription plans) assigned to that user
The number of devices they own
Their job title in Active Directory
quiz.why: Capabilities such as Exchange Online, Teams, and Copilot are unlocked per user by the licences assigned to them; a user with no licence has no access to those services.

quiz.q: Where are user identities and sign-in stored for a Microsoft 365 tenant?
quiz.why: Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure AD) is the identity and access layer for the tenant; it holds user accounts, groups, and the sign-in/authentication that all M365 services rely on.

quiz.q: Name the default domain every new Microsoft 365 tenant receives, and why an organisation usually adds a custom one.
quiz.answer: Every tenant gets a default domain in the form yourcompany.onmicrosoft.com; organisations add a custom domain (like contoso.com) so user sign-in and email addresses look professional and match their brand.
quiz.why: The onmicrosoft.com domain always works as a fallback, but custom domains require verifying DNS records and are what users actually sign in and send mail with.

quiz.q: In one sentence, why should you avoid handing out the Global Administrator role to everyone who needs to make a change?
quiz.answer: Global Administrator can change anything in the tenant, so granting it widely is a major security risk; you should assign the least-privileged role that lets each admin do their specific job.
quiz.why: Least privilege limits blast radius — if a Help Desk admin only needs to reset passwords, give them the Helpdesk Administrator role, not full Global Admin.

body_markdown:
## What a tenant really is

When an organisation buys Microsoft 365, Microsoft creates a **tenant** for them: a dedicated, logically isolated instance of all the cloud services — identity, email, Teams, SharePoint, security tooling — that belongs only to that organisation. Your company's tenant is separate from every other company's, even though they all run on the same Microsoft cloud.

Every tenant has a unique **tenant ID** (a GUID) and a default domain in the form `yourcompany.onmicrosoft.com`. As a Tier 2 admin, the tenant is the boundary you work inside all day.

## The admin centers

You manage the tenant through a set of web portals. The hub is the **Microsoft 365 admin center** at `admin.microsoft.com`, where you handle users, groups, licences, and service health, and from which you jump to the specialist portals.

```text
Microsoft 365 admin center (admin.microsoft.com)
  +-- Exchange admin center        (email)
  +-- Teams admin center           (meetings, calling)
  +-- SharePoint admin center      (sites, OneDrive)
  +-- Microsoft Entra admin center (identity)
  +-- Microsoft Purview            (compliance)
  +-- Microsoft Defender portal    (security)
```

Knowing which portal owns which job is half the battle when a ticket lands.

## Identity and domains

Underneath everything sits **Microsoft Entra ID** (formerly Azure AD). It stores user accounts, groups, and the **authentication** that every service trusts. When a user signs in to Outlook, Teams, or SharePoint, Entra ID is what verifies them.

Most organisations add a **custom domain** like `contoso.com` so that sign-in names and email addresses look professional. Adding a domain means verifying ownership through DNS records — typically a TXT record to prove control, then MX and other records so mail flows.

## Licensing: what unlocks what

A tenant subscribes to one or more **plans** (for example Microsoft 365 Business Premium or E3/E5). Each plan is a bundle of **licences** that unlock specific services. You assign licences **per user** — a user with no Exchange licence has no mailbox; a user with no Copilot licence cannot use Copilot.

When a user reports "I can't get to Teams" your first reflex should be to check their assigned licences in the admin center before you touch anything else.

## Roles and least privilege

Not every admin needs full power. **Admin roles** decide who can change what. The **Global Administrator** role can do everything — which is exactly why you give it to very few people. For day-to-day support, narrower roles like **Helpdesk Administrator** (reset passwords) or **User Administrator** (manage users) follow the principle of **least privilege**: grant the smallest role that does the job.

```text
Admin center > Roles > Role assignments
  - Find the role (e.g. Helpdesk Administrator)
  - Assign the specific user
  - Review assignments regularly
```

## Your task

Sign in to a Microsoft 365 admin center (use a free Microsoft 365 Developer tenant if you don't have one). Find and write down your tenant's default `.onmicrosoft.com` domain and tenant ID, list which specialist admin centers you can reach from the hub, and note which admin role you would assign to a Tier 1 colleague who only needs to reset passwords.

slides.title: Microsoft 365 tenant overview
slides.narration: Welcome to Month Six. You've come a long way, and now we're consolidating everything into cloud administration with Microsoft 365, aligned to the M S one oh two administrator certification. This first lesson is the lay of the land: what a tenant actually is, how the admin centers fit together, and where you go to support users. Get this mental map right and everything that follows clicks into place.

slides.title: What is a tenant?
bullets: A dedicated, isolated instance of Microsoft 365 for one org.
Separate from every other company's tenant.
Has a unique tenant ID (a GUID).
Default domain: yourcompany.onmicrosoft.com.
slides.narration: Let's start with the word you'll hear all day: tenant. When an organisation buys Microsoft 365, Microsoft spins up a dedicated, isolated instance of all the cloud services just for them. That's the tenant. Your company's tenant is walled off from every other company's, even though they share the same cloud. Each one has a unique tenant I D and a default domain ending in dot onmicrosoft dot com. The tenant is the boundary you work inside every single day.

slides.title: The admin centers
bullets: Hub: Microsoft 365 admin center at admin.microsoft.com.
Specialist portals: Exchange, Teams, SharePoint.
Plus Entra, Purview, and Defender.
Knowing which portal owns the job is half the battle.
slides.code:
Microsoft 365 admin center (admin.microsoft.com)
  +-- Exchange admin center        (email)
  +-- Teams admin center           (meetings, calling)
  +-- SharePoint admin center      (sites, OneDrive)
  +-- Microsoft Entra admin center (identity)
  +-- Microsoft Purview            (compliance)
  +-- Microsoft Defender portal    (security)
slides.narration: You manage the tenant through web portals. The hub is the Microsoft 365 admin center at admin dot microsoft dot com. From there you handle users, licences, and service health, and you jump out to the specialist portals: Exchange for email, Teams for meetings and calling, SharePoint for sites, Entra for identity, Purview for compliance, and Defender for security. When a ticket lands, knowing which portal owns the problem is genuinely half the battle.

slides.title: Identity with Entra ID
bullets: Microsoft Entra ID is the identity layer.
Stores user accounts, groups, and sign-in.
Every service trusts Entra to authenticate users.
Formerly known as Azure AD.
slides.narration: Underneath all of it sits Microsoft Entra I D, which you may still hear called Azure A D. This is the identity layer. It stores the user accounts, the groups, and the authentication that every other service trusts. When someone signs in to Outlook or Teams, it's Entra that checks who they are. Identity is the foundation everything else stands on, so we'll spend the whole next lesson on it.

slides.title: Domains and DNS
bullets: Default domain always works as a fallback.
Custom domains (contoso.com) look professional.
Adding one means verifying DNS records.
TXT to prove ownership, MX so mail flows.
slides.narration: Every tenant gets that dot onmicrosoft dot com domain, and it always works as a fallback. But organisations add a custom domain, like contoso dot com, so sign-in names and email addresses look professional. Adding a domain means proving you own it through D N S records: typically a T X T record to verify ownership, then M X and other records so mail actually flows. You'll see this dance whenever a company is onboarded.

slides.title: Licensing unlocks services
bullets: The tenant subscribes to plans like Business Premium or E5.
Each plan bundles licences that unlock services.
Licences are assigned per user.
No licence means no access to that service.
slides.narration: Here's a concept that explains a huge share of your tickets: licensing. The tenant subscribes to plans, things like Business Premium or E three and E five. Each plan bundles licences that unlock specific services. And crucially, you assign those licences per user. A user with no Exchange licence has no mailbox. No Copilot licence, no Copilot. So when someone says I can't get into Teams, your very first reflex should be to check their assigned licences before you touch anything else.

slides.title: Admin roles and least privilege
bullets: Global Administrator can change everything.
So you give it to very few people.
Helpdesk Admin resets passwords; User Admin manages users.
Least privilege: grant the smallest role that works.
slides.narration: Not every admin needs the keys to the kingdom. Admin roles decide who can change what. The Global Administrator role can do absolutely everything, which is precisely why you hand it out to very few people. For day-to-day support there are narrower roles: Helpdesk Administrator just resets passwords, User Administrator manages users. The principle here is least privilege: always grant the smallest role that lets the person do their job. It limits the damage if an account is ever compromised.

slides.title: Where you actually work
bullets: Find a user, check licences, check sign-in.
Pick the right portal for the service.
Use the right role to make the change.
The tenant is your workspace boundary.
slides.code:
Admin center > Roles > Role assignments
  - Find the role (e.g. Helpdesk Administrator)
  - Assign the specific user
  - Review assignments regularly
slides.narration: Putting it together, here's how your day flows. A ticket arrives. You find the user, check their licences and sign-in. You pick the right portal for whichever service is misbehaving. And you make the change using the appropriate admin role, not the biggest one you happen to have. Role assignments live under Roles in the admin center. Get into the habit of reviewing them regularly so privilege doesn't quietly creep upward.

slides.title: Recap & your task
bullets: A tenant is one org's isolated M365 instance.
Admin centers: hub plus specialist portals.
Entra ID is identity; licences unlock services.

slides.narration: Let's recap. A tenant is one organisation's dedicated, isolated instance of Microsoft 365. You manage it through the admin center hub and its specialist portals. Entra I D handles identity, licences unlock services per user, and you make changes using least-privilege admin roles. Your task: sign in to an admin center, ideally a free developer tenant, and write down your default onmicrosoft domain and tenant I D, list the specialist portals you can reach, and decide which role you'd give a Tier One colleague who only needs to reset passwords. See you in the next lesson, where we go deep on identity.
